lecture.title: MIT 6.0001 (Fall 2016) Lecture 10: Understanding Program Efficiency, Part 1
lecture.attribution: Eric Grimson, John Guttag and Ana Bell. 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python, Fall 2016. MIT OpenCourseWare.

status: draft: spans taken from the official captions, not yet checked against the video

questions.question: What two kinds of efficiency does the lecture mention, and which one does it focus on?
questions.answer: Time and space (memory). The lecture and the next one focus on time.

questions.question: If computers keep getting faster, why should I still care how efficient my code is?
questions.answer: Because the problems grow faster than the hardware: data sets are becoming massive, so a naive algorithm stays too slow.

questions.question: How much did Google serve in 2014, according to the lecture?
questions.answer: About 30 trillion web pages, covering 100 million gigabytes of data.

questions.question: What earlier example traded memory for speed?
questions.answer: Computing Fibonacci with a dictionary that stores intermediate values, which greatly reduces the time.

questions.question: What three approaches to measuring an algorithm's efficiency are compared?
questions.answer: Timing the code, counting operations, and the more abstract order of growth.

questions.question: Which function from the time module is used to time a function call?
questions.answer: time.clock: call it before and after the function and take the difference.

questions.question: Why isn't measuring how long my program runs a good way to compare algorithms?
questions.answer: Running time also depends on the implementation and on the computer, and timings on small inputs don't predict large ones.

questions.question: What counts as a primitive operation when counting steps?
questions.answer: Arithmetic, comparisons, assignments and retrieving values from memory, each assumed to take the same constant time.

questions.question: How many operations does the loop that adds up the integers from 0 to x take?
questions.answer: 1 + 3x, or 3x + 2 counting the return.

questions.question: How many operations does the summing function take when x is 1,000?
What happens to the operation count if the for loop is rewritten as a while loop?
questions.answer: Each iteration gains an operation (setting and testing i), so 3x + 1 becomes 4x + 1: counting still depends on the implementation.

questions.question: What are the best, average and worst cases when searching a list for an element?
questions.answer: Best: the element is first, so the time doesn't depend on the length. Average: about half the list. Worst: the element isn't there and every item is checked.

questions.question: Why analyse the unluckiest input rather than the typical one?
questions.answer: The worst case gives an upper bound on the time, and it's often the bottleneck.

questions.question: If the list doubles in length, what happens to the worst-case time of a linear search?
questions.answer: It doubles; ten times longer takes ten times as long. The relationship is linear.

questions.question: Where does the name Big O come from?
questions.answer: The professor thinks it comes from the Greek letter omicron.

questions.question: How many steps does the iterative factorial function take?
questions.answer: 5n + 2, which is order n.

questions.question: Why are additive and multiplicative constants ignored in orders of growth?
questions.answer: Orders of growth describe behaviour as n gets very large, where the constants don't matter, so only the fastest-growing term counts.

questions.question: What is the order of growth of n squared plus 2n plus 2?
questions.answer: Order n squared.

questions.question: Which grows faster: n to the 30th or 3 to the n?
questions.answer: 3 to the n: exponentials eventually beat any power.

questions.question: Is logarithmic growth better or worse than linear growth?
questions.answer: Better: a logarithm grows more and more slowly as the input grows.

questions.question: Where does n log n sit compared with linear and quadratic growth?
questions.answer: Between them. Log-linear is common for valuable algorithms and behaves well.

questions.question: What is the law of addition for orders of growth?
questions.answer: For code run one piece after another, O(f) + O(g) is O(f + g). A linear loop followed by a quadratic one is O(n squared).

questions.question: What is the law of multiplication for orders of growth?
questions.answer: For nested code, multiply the orders of growth of the inner and outer parts: two nested loops over n are O(n squared).

questions.question: Who does the professor impersonate while printing A in a nested loop?
questions.answer: The Fonz, saying "heyyy".

questions.question: Why does putting a loop inside another loop usually make code quadratic?
questions.answer: The inner loop does order n work for each of the outer loop's n iterations, so n times n.

questions.question: By how much does log n grow when the input grows tenfold?
questions.answer: By about a factor of 2 from 10 to 100, then only about 50% more for the next factor of ten.

questions.question: What should you bring if your algorithm is at the bottom of the complexity table?
questions.answer: A sleeping bag and some coffee: you'll be waiting a long time.

questions.question: Does returning True as soon as the element is found change the order of growth of linear search?
questions.answer: No. It lowers the average time, but in the worst case (the element isn't there) every item is still checked, so it stays order n.

questions.question: How can Python reach any element of a list in constant time?
questions.answer: Elements sit in consecutive memory, so element i is at the base address plus i times the element size. For mixed types, the list stores pointers (indirection).

questions.question: Does a sorted list make linear search faster in terms of order of growth?
questions.answer: No. The search can stop once items are bigger than the target, which helps on average, but the worst case is still order n.

questions.question: What is the complexity of adding up the digits in a string?
questions.answer: Linear in the length of the string: one loop with constant work per character.

questions.question: What is the worst-case complexity of checking whether one list is a subset of another?
questions.answer: Quadratic: length of L1 times length of L2, worst when the lists are the same length and share no elements.

questions.question: Why is the second loop of the intersection function also quadratic?
questions.answer: Checking whether an element is in a list is itself a loop over the list, so the second loop hides a nested loop.
